title: Quantum Partial Information Decompositions, an Operational Order on Ensembles, and Direct Quantifications of Objective Information
abstract: The partial information decomposition (PID) framework is an extension of classical information theory that enables a systematic analysis of the structure of information in multipartite systems. We advance a simple extension of this framework enabling the construction of multipartite quantum PIDs (QPIDs); generalizing recent, exclusively bipartite, extensions. We construct two QPIDs of the Holevo quantity. First a naive QPID based on the classical minimum mutual information. Second a sophisticated QPID enabled by our development of an operational partial order on quantum ensembles in terms of ensemble (inter-)convertability. Finally, as a concrete example of how QPIDs can be applied, we investigate objectivity scenarios; using our Holevo QPIDs to directly quantify objective information in extended graph states. These findings ultimately establish a foundation upon which generic multipartite QPIDs can be systematically constructed, introduce an operational partial order on ensembles, advance QPIDs as interesting objects of study in their own right, and demonstrate their immediate applicability to problems in quantum information.
summary: This paper generalizes the Partial Information Decomposition (PID) framework to multipartite quantum systems, creating Quantum Partial Information Decompositions (QPIDs). By defining an operational partial order on quantum ensembles, the authors construct sophisticated QPIDs for quantities like the Holevo information. These tools allow for the systematic quantification of objective information in complex quantum states, establishing a new foundation for quantum information analysis.
main_problem: The paper aims to extend the Partial Information Decomposition (PID) framework from classical to multipartite quantum systems (QPIDs) to systematically analyze the structure of quantum information.
main_result: The authors construct a sophisticated QPID for the Holevo quantity based on an operational partial order on quantum ensembles, demonstrating its immediate applicability to quantifying objective information in extended graph states.
method: The core method involves developing a set-theoretic decomposition based on antichains of source subsets, coupled with defining an operational partial order on quantum ensembles via ensemble (inter-)convertibility.
model_or_system: The analysis is performed on multipartite quantum systems, using extended graph states (like the 'twisted parachute' state) as a concrete example to quantify objective information.
key_observables: Quantum Partial Information Decompositions (QPIDs), the Holevo quantity, and the deviation $\Delta\chi^{(\alpha^{\perp})}$ quantifying the difference between naive and sophisticated redundancy estimates.
main_assumptions: The choice of the redundancy function $\chi_{\cap}(\alpha)$ is non-unique and problem-specific; the sophisticated QPID requires solving nested, non-convex optimization problems.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematics of the PID set-theoretic construction, the ensemble conversion procedure, and show how the deviation $\Delta\chi^{(\alpha^{\perp})}$ scales with system size $N$ and scrambling $\phi$.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the general set-theoretic PID framework, then extends it to the quantum domain (QPIDs) using an operational partial order on ensembles. Finally, it applies these tools to quantify objective information in specific quantum states.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, information-theoretic tool (QPIDs) to quantify structural redundancies and objective information in complex quantum multipartite systems, which is highly relevant for understanding quantum correlations beyond simple entanglement measures.

Schematics showing (a) the structure of three sets rel- evant to the set-theoretic construction of the PID framework, example elements of these sets are shown as nodes, and par- tial orderings under the relevant relation are shown as directed arrows (i.e. P ⊆Q as P →Q or β ≼α as β →α). (b) a pro- cedure by which one ensemble can be turned into another via quantum operations E and classical message aggregation G. (c) the ‘twisted parachute’ graph state, an anisotropic model displaying objective (fine-grained, redundant) information.

FIG. 2. Processing-inferiority error ε for a variety of illustra- tive input (η) and output (µ) qubit ensembles, as a function of iterations (both G and E) of the see-saw SDP scheme. In- sets schematically show z-x Bloch planes corresponding to the ensembles studied in each panel, with the input, output, and optimal µopt ensembles superimposed. Forward results µ ≼p.i. η shown for three backend solvers (SCS, CLARABEL, and MOSEK), and additional inverse result η ≼p.i. µ shown for MOSEK. Exact details of the toy ensembles studied in each sub-panel (a)-(f) are given in Table II.

FIG. 3. Processing-inferiority error ε (panels (a)-(c)) and Holevo quantity χ (panel (d)) landscapes for rA = rB = r and p = 1/2 planes of generic (2,2)-ensembles. Solving for the processing-inferior redundant capacity χ(2) ∩ involves simultaneous optimization over all landscapes. Superimposed markers identify the solution to this optimization problem for three indicative tolerances ε ≤10−10, 10−6, and 10−2.

FIG. 4. Information atoms χ(1) ∂(α) resulting from the bipar- tite QPID using the minimum redundant capacity χ(1) ∩ as a function of environment fractions NA/N. Panels show all atoms for both weak ϕ = 0.05π and strong ϕ = 0.95π scram- bling; for (a) no twisting ∆= 0, and (b) twisting ∆= 0.1, respectively. Plateaux characteristic of quantum darwinism can be seen in the redundancy atom χ(1) ∂(α⊥).

Main panel shows χ(1) ∩(α⊥) and χ(2) ∩(α⊥) of the N = 12 twisted parachute state with finite encoding errors and twisting δθ = ∆= 0.1 for the lowest (maximally redundant) antichain α⊥as a func- tion of scrambling ϕ.
